title: gLLM: Global Balanced Pipeline Parallelism Systems for Distributed LLMs Serving with Token Throttling
problem: Pipeline parallelism for LLM serving exhibits pipeline bubbles from imbalanced computation across batches; hybrid scheduling (Sarathi-Serve) with fixed token budgets creates fluctuations from insufficient/uneven token distribution, causing computational imbalance and reduced throughput.
motivation: LLM inference at scale requires pipeline parallelism across distributed nodes to minimize communication overhead vs tensor parallelism. However, pipeline bubbles (idle compute stages) significantly reduce effective throughput and utilization.
method: gLLM uses token throttling—controlling how many input and output tokens flow through each pipeline stage—to independently regulate the prefill phase (processing input) and decode phase (generating output). The decode phase has relatively consistent computational cost, so keeping it balanced prevents GPU idle time; prefill has variable cost depending on input size, so it adjusts dynamically based on queue depth (how many requests are waiting) and available KV cache memory (storage for precomputed values). This independent regulation, coordinated via asynchronous message passing, prevents the computation imbalances that occur with fixed token budgets.
key_novelty: gLLM independently throttles prefill and decode token quantities, dynamically adjusting based on queue depth and KV cache memory instead of using a fixed token budget across the pipeline.
contributions: Token Throttling mechanism reducing pipeline bubbles through fine-grained scheduling
Independent prefill/decode token regulation enabling balanced computation
Dynamic batch sizing based on KV cache memory utilization
Asynchronous execution architecture optimized for pipeline parallelism
11-398% higher maximum throughput vs state-of-the-art pipeline/tensor parallelism systems
baselines: Sarathi-Serve (hybrid scheduling with fixed token budget)
limitations: Evaluation limited to representative LLMs (details sparse)
Wide throughput improvement range (11-398%) suggests workload-dependent variability
Abstract-only prevents assessment of latency/throughput tradeoff curves
KV cache memory pressure handling details limited
Open-source code availability reduces reproducibility barriers but implementation details sparse
primary_theme: LLM inference serving via token-aware pipeline scheduling
